newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Split among Bosnian Serbs worries Western envoys.
newsitem.headline: Split among Bosnian Serbs worries Western envoys.

text.p: Western mediators expressed concern on Tuesday over mounting tensions between rival Serb factions in Bosnia after a police chief was detained by hardline state security men.
"The situation is a critical one. There is a clear split," the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp, told reporters in Sarajevo.

Westendorp said major powers were worried about the conflict pitting Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic against government hardliners loyal to ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.

Plavsic's newly-appointed police chief in the northern town of Banja Luka, Milan Sutilovic, and his deputy were detained on Tuesday morning by state security agents. The two men were released after they refused demands to resign.

The U.S. envoy to former Yugoslavia, Robert Gelbard, cancelled scheduled meetings in the capital Sarajevo and flew by helicopter to Banja Luka to hold crisis talks with Plavsic on Tuesday evening, diplomats said.

The brief detention of the Banja Luka police chief came two days after special police units loyal to Plavsic seized control of a police station which they said was being used to mount elaborate telephone tapping of the president's office.
NATO peacekeeping troops in armoured vehicles surrounded the building on Sunday to prevent a clash between Plavsic's special police and forces deployed by hardliners.
International police monitors searched the building and found more than 500 tapes and sophisticated eavesdropping equipment in the building, Western officials said.
Plavsic has alleged that Karadzic loyalists were tapping the telephones of dozens of officials and prominent figures in Banja Luka, including two judges on the constitutional court.
Westendorp said his office "deplored" reports that Karadzic loyalists had intimidated the court judges. One of the judges was badly beaten last week.
Government hardliners had pushed the court to strike down Plavsic's decision last month to dissolve parliament and call early elections in Bosnia's autonomous Serb territory.
The detention on Tuesday reflected attempts by both factions to establish clear control over the police force, the main lever used by Karadzic's allies to rule Serb territory.
NATO officers said the alliance-led peace force would not tolerate any violence between rival police factions but diplomats were concerned that the crisis could drag on without resolution.
Plavsic has accused Karadzic and his hardline nationalist allies of rampant corruption and of damaging Serb interests by blocking the peace process.
Although Plavsic is nationalist ideologue, Western governments view her as a pragmatic partner who is more willing to abide by the terms of the 1995 Dayton peace agreement.
The turmoil has refocused international attention on Karadzic's covert political influence and his refusal to face trial before the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
United States officials have said they will not tolerate Karadzic undermining the peace process indefinitely and have hinted that the wartime leader might be snatched at some point by NATO troops.

Karadzic has been indicted by the U.N. tribunal for crimes against humanity linked to the brutal siege of Sarajevo, ethnic purges of Moslems and Croats and the slaughter of thousands of Moslem men from the Srebrenica enclave.
